ns_the_spot_g_spot.blurb: A small granite crag in forest near Musquodoboit Harbour, east of Halifax, and a popular first stop for climbers learning to lead in Nova Scotia. Most of the thirty climbs are bolted slabs and faces, with a smaller group of crack lines to protect yourself. Grades cluster in the middle: plenty of 5.8 to 5.11, a few easier lines, and a single 5.12. Holds on the slabs are generally large and positive. The cliff is stepped in several tiers, shady and breezy in the trees, with glimpses of the sea. The walk in is short but over uneven ground, and low sections of trail can flood in spring. Carry out everything and leave the rock unmarked.

va_hidden_roofs.blurb: A west-facing sandstone crag in the George Washington National Forest, southwest of Harrisonburg in Rockingham County. It is the newer, steeper section of the Hidden Rocks complex, known for big roofs and the tallest lines in the county. Nearly all of the thirty-odd climbs are bolted, with a handful of trad lines and two top-ropes. Grades run from easy 5.6s up into the 5.13 range, with the bulk between 5.9 and 5.12. It can be windy. Recent cleaning removed much loose rock, but a helmet is still wise. Expect a long hike with several stream crossings, so it is quiet compared with better-known Virginia areas. Nearby taller cliffs on private land are closed to climbing.
va_hidden_roofs.parking_note: Parking is in pull-offs along Hone Quarry Road in the national forest, which also has a basic campground. Use the first lot for the hike to the older Hidden crags, then continue past them on foot.
va_hidden_roofs.approach: From the trailhead on Hone Quarry Road, hike to the older Hidden crags, then keep going past the end of the obvious trail. The route crosses the stream several times, which is slow in high water; the longer way up the creek bed is easier avoided then. You can walk up to the clifftop at both the left and right ends.

va_springfield_bouldering_hooes_rd.blurb: A small, urban boulder site beside Accotink Creek in Springfield, Fairfax County, mostly used by local climbers after work. About thirty problems on granite, with a wide spread: a lot of V0 to V4, a middle run of V5 to V8, and a few very hard lines at the top end. Some overhanging problems are steep and tall enough that a couple of pads and a spotter help. A vertical face on the parkway side has a bolted top-rope anchor. It stays dry most of the time, which suits winter and wet days. Glass and graffiti have been cleaned up in volunteer work days, but check landings and topouts before committing.
va_springfield_bouldering_hooes_rd.parking_note: Park at the roadside pull-off on Hooes Road just past the small bridge over Accotink Creek. Space is limited, so carpool, and keep to the edge of the road when walking.
va_springfield_bouldering_hooes_rd.approach: A short trail leaves the road beside the creek and reaches the boulders after roughly 60 yards. Walk single file along the road shoulder to get to it.

va_lodges.blurb: A sport-only wall in Breaks Interstate Park, in far southwest Virginia on the Kentucky line, sitting just beside the Towers. All thirty routes are bolted, and the grades start around 5.9 and run through the 5.10s and 5.11s into a good block of 5.12s, with a few 5.13s, so it suits stronger climbers more than beginners. It is sunny, and some lines seep for about a day after rain or snowmelt. Visitors need to follow the park's climbing rules, including a free waiver each calendar year, and climb only in approved areas. The trail to the wall is flagged, and it is easy to wander onto the separate Lower Lodges path by mistake.

wa_main_wall_7.blurb: The tallest and most popular wall at Minnehaha, a granite crag in John H. Shields Park on the Spokane River in northeast Spokane. Roughly fifty climbs, mostly traditional lines with a good group of bolted routes and a few boulder problems. Grades are broad: easy crack climbs at 5.5 to 5.7 up through many 5.8 to 5.10 routes and a solid number of 5.11s, with a handful harder. Rock is coarse and friendly on the fingertips. The wall has both sunny and shaded sections, can be busy, and every route can be top-roped. It sits very close to the parking lot, so it is an easy after-work or half-day trip.
wa_main_wall_7.approach: The base of the wall is only a short stroll from the park lot, a minute or two on a clear path.

wa_west_face_7.blurb: The sunset-facing side of Beacon Rock, the big basalt monolith on the Washington bank of the Columbia Gorge. Most of the forty-odd routes are columnar trad lines, with a good number of bolted sport climbs and a few aid routes. Grades run from about 5.7 through the 5.10s and 5.11s, with a few 5.12s, so bring a full rack. The west side stays open all year, unlike the south face, which closes in late winter and spring for nesting falcons. Wear a helmet for rockfall and watch for poison oak, especially on the trail down to the wall. The climbers' path branches off the main hiking trail, and the base has rough belay platforms.
